The iPhone 17 can handle just about everything, streaming, navigation, work apps, even gaming on the go. But with that kind of daily use, keeping your battery topped up becomes part of the routine.

Benefits of Using MagSafe Chargers

MagSafe chargers make everyday charging feel a lot simpler. Instead of adjusting your phone to find the right spot like with standard wireless chargers, the magnets guide it into place instantly, so it starts charging as soon as it connects.

That alignment also helps with consistency. Since the charging coil stays in the correct position, you’re less likely to deal with slow or interrupted charging, which can happen with regular wireless pads.

Another advantage is flexibility. Many MagSafe chargers are designed to handle more than just your phone, letting you charge your iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch in one setup. It keeps your space cleaner and makes charging easier whether you’re at your desk, bedside, or packing for a trip.

Key Features to Look for in the Best MagSafe Chargers

Before choosing a MagSafe charger for your iPhone 17, it helps to focus on the features that actually affect your daily experience. The right combination can make charging feel effortless instead of something you have to think about.

Qi2 Certification / Fast Charging

Faster wireless charging speeds
More precise magnetic alignment
Better energy efficiency

In everyday use, that translates to more consistent charging and less time waiting around for your battery to catch up.

Active Heat Management

Wireless charging naturally creates heat, especially during faster charging sessions. Good MagSafe chargers include built-in heat management to keep temperatures under control. This helps:

Reduce the risk of overheating
Keep charging performance stable
Support better battery health over time

It’s especially useful if you charge your phone overnight or leave it on the charger for extended periods.

Strong Magnetic Hold

One of the main advantages of MagSafe is how easily it snaps into place, but not all chargers feel the same. A strong magnetic hold keeps your phone securely attached and properly aligned while charging. This helps:

Maintain consistent charging performance
Prevent the phone from slipping out of position
Avoid interruptions during use

iPhone

These small design choices help keep your phone secure and make the charger more comfortable to use.

Portability and Versatility

Safety Features

Safety is something you don’t want to overlook. Reliable MagSafe chargers include built-in protections such as:

Temperature control
Foreign object detection

These features help keep charging stable and protect both your iPhone and the charger from potential issues over time.

How to Choose the Right MagSafe Charger for iPhone 17

With several types of MagSafe chargers available, the best choice usually comes down to where and how you plan to use it. Some work better on a desk or nightstand, while others are designed for travel or handling multiple devices at once.

Thinking about your daily habits, where you charge, how often, and what devices you use can make the decision much more straightforward.

Choosing a Charger for Home or Office Use

For home or office setups, stability and ease of use tend to matter most. Chargers that hold your phone upright make it easier to glance at notifications, take calls, or use StandBy mode while charging.

They’re a good fit because they:

Keep your phone securely in place
Provide a comfortable viewing angle
Help maintain a clean, organized setup

A multi-device charging station can also simplify things by reducing the number of cables on your desk or nightstand.

Selecting a Travel-Friendly MagSafe Charger

If you travel often, portability becomes a bigger priority. Larger charging stations may work well at home, but they’re not always practical to pack. Travel-friendly options are designed to be easier to carry and set up wherever you are.

A compact size that fits easily in a bag

Enough flexibility for different charging situations

Charging pads or portable magnetic power banks are often the most convenient choices when space is limited.

Considering Multi-Device Charging Needs

Choosing the right setup depends on how many devices you charge regularly and whether you prefer everything in one place.

For example:

High output chargers focus on faster charging

Multi-device setups emphasize convenience

The right choice depends on what fits your routine best.

Final Thoughts: The Best MagSafe Chargers for iPhone 17

Choosing the best MagSafe charger for iPhone 17 really comes down to how you charge your phone day to day. Some setups work better for a desk or nightstand, while others are more useful when you’re traveling or managing multiple devices.

Once you narrow down what matters, whether it’s charging speed, magnetic stability, or overall design, it becomes easier to find something that fits naturally into your routine. The right charger doesn’t just keep your phone powered; it makes the whole experience feel more consistent and effortless throughout the day.

MagSafe Charger FAQ for iPhone 17
Do MagSafe chargers work with iPhone 17?

Yes, MagSafe chargers are fully compatible with the iPhone 17. The built-in magnets help align the charger with the phone’s charging coil automatically, so it connects easily and charges more consistently than standard wireless chargers.

What is the fastest MagSafe charging speed for iPhone 17?

The fastest MagSafe wireless charging speed for iPhone 17 is typically up to 25W when using a compatible MagSafe or Qi2-certified charger with the right power adapter. Standard wireless chargers without magnetic alignment usually charge at lower speeds and may not be as consistent.

Can MagSafe chargers charge AirPods and other Apple devices?

Yes, many MagSafe chargers can also charge AirPods with wireless charging cases. Some models, especially 2-in-1 or 3-in-1 setups, are designed to charge multiple devices at once, including:

iPhone
AirPods
Apple Watch

This makes them a convenient option if you use multiple Apple devices daily.

Are MagSafe chargers safe for long-term battery health?

Yes, as long as you’re using a well-built charger with proper safety features. Most modern MagSafe chargers include temperature control, power regulation, and foreign object detection. These features help keep charging stable and reduce the risk of overheating over time.

Do you need a special adapter for MagSafe chargers?

Most MagSafe chargers use a USB-C power adapter, and the charging speed depends on its output. For faster charging, a 30W or higher adapter is usually recommended. Lower power adapters can still work, but charging speeds may be slower.

iPhone Wireless Fast Charge Guide: What Actually Works in 2026 
 iPhone Wireless Fast Charge Guide: What Actually Works in 2026
 21 July 2026 
 By Alex Morgan 
 Want to explore more about this article? Try the ask below
 →
 If you want real speed from iPhone wireless charging in 2026, prioritize Qi2.2-certified, magnetically aligned chargers with active thermal management — not just any ‘25W’ label. Skip non-magnetic pads, avoid unventilated designs, and don’t assume older 15W Qi1 accessories will deliver fast results. Over the past year, the shift to Qi2.2 (25W) has redefined expectations: iPhones now reach 80% in ~50 minutes 1 . That’s only possible with precise coil alignment and heat control — meaning your choice isn’t about wattage alone, but hardware synergy. If you’re a typical user, you don’t need to overthink this: go for a certified Qi2.2 station with MagSafe-compatible magnets and passive or active cooling. This piece isn’t for keyword collectors. It’s for people who will actually use the product. 
 About iPhone Wireless Fast Charge
 “iPhone wireless fast charge” refers to wireless power delivery that consistently delivers ≥15W to compatible iPhones (iPhone 15 Pro and newer), enabling meaningful battery replenishment in under an hour. Unlike standard Qi1 (7.5W) or legacy MagSafe (15W), true fast wireless charging in 2026 means leveraging the Qi2.2 standard , which enables up to 25W output while maintaining interoperability and safety protocols 2 . It requires three things working together: (1) an iPhone 17/18 Pro (or iPhone 15/16 Pro with firmware updates), (2) a Qi2.2-certified transmitter, and (3) magnetic alignment — not optional, but foundational.
 Typical use cases include desk-based charging during work hours, overnight bedside top-ups, or multi-device stations for iPhone + Apple Watch + AirPods. It’s not designed for on-the-go portability like wired PD, nor does it replace high-power USB-C charging for rapid recovery after heavy use. But for consistent, hands-free replenishment — especially when paired with active cooling — it now delivers measurable time savings.
 Why iPhone Wireless Fast Charge Is Gaining Popularity
 Lately, search interest for “iphone wireless fast charge” surged dramatically — peaking at 27 on Google Trends in April 2026, coinciding with the launch of third-party Qi2.2-certified chargers 1 . This isn’t just hype. The driver is functional: users are tired of waiting 2+ hours for a full wireless charge. With Qi2.2, 80% in ~50 minutes changes behavior — it becomes viable for lunch-break top-ups or pre-meeting boosts.
 Three concrete shifts explain the momentum:
 🔋 Speed parity with wired convenience: No cable fumbling, yet near-wired speed — if thermal throttling is avoided.
 🧲 Magnetic alignment as baseline expectation: 100% of top-performing search queries include “magnetic” or “snap-on” 3 . Users now associate loose placement with inefficiency — and rightly so.
 🌡️ Thermal awareness rising: Consumers report abandoning early 25W attempts due to heat-induced slowdowns. That’s why active cooling (e.g., CryoBoost fans) and vented chassis appear in >60% of top-reviewed 2026 models 1 .
 Qi2.2 25W chargers feature integrated magnetic rings and thermal vents — design cues now essential for performance. 
 Approaches and Differences
 There are three dominant approaches to iPhone wireless fast charging in 2026 — each with clear trade-offs:
 1. Single-Device Qi2.2 Pads (Magnetic)
 Pros: Highest efficiency (minimal coil misalignment), compact footprint, lowest price point ($45–$75), easiest thermal management.
 Cons: Charges one device only; limited positioning flexibility; no built-in watch or earbud charging.
 When it’s worth caring about: You prioritize speed, reliability, and minimal desk clutter — especially if you charge only your iPhone daily.
 When you don’t need to overthink it: If you already own a MagSafe-compatible case and don’t need multi-device support, this is the simplest path. If you’re a typical user, you don’t need to overthink this.
 2. 3-in-1 Magnetic Charging Stations
 Pros: Consolidates iPhone + Watch + AirPods; Qi2.2 power routing often prioritizes iPhone first; modern units integrate active cooling.
 Cons: Higher cost ($99–$179); larger footprint; thermal load increases with simultaneous charging; some models throttle iPhone speed when Watch/AirPods draw power.
 When it’s worth caring about: You value clean desk setup and routinely charge all three devices — and your workflow supports fixed-location charging.
 When you don’t need to overthink it: If you rarely charge your Watch or AirPods overnight, or if your desk space is tight, the added complexity and cost offer diminishing returns.
 3. Non-Magnetic or Qi1-Only Pads (Even Labeled ‘25W’)
 Pros: Lower price ($25–$40); widely available.
 Cons: Cannot sustain >7.5W on iPhone without precise manual alignment; no Qi2.2 certification; zero thermal safeguards for sustained output; prone to throttling within 3–5 minutes.
 When it’s worth caring about: Never — unless you’re testing compatibility or using it solely for Android devices.
 When you don’t need to overthink it: Avoid entirely. Marketing labels like “25W Max” on non-Qi2.2 pads are misleading — they reflect theoretical peak under lab conditions, not real-world iPhone throughput.
 Key Features and Specifications to Evaluate
 Don’t default to wattage alone. Here’s what matters — and why:
 ✅ Qi2.2 Certification (not just ‘Qi2’ or ‘Qi’): Qi2.2 adds mandatory power negotiation and enhanced thermal reporting. Qi2-only units may still cap at 15W. Look for the official Qi2.2 logo — not marketing copy.
 🧲 Magnetic Alignment Strength (≥ 25 N pull force): Weak magnets cause micro-shifts during charging, triggering power drops. Verified pull-force specs matter more than “MagSafe compatible” claims.
 🌬️ Cooling Method: Passive (aluminum chassis + vents) works for single-device use. Active (low-noise fan + temperature sensor) is essential for 3-in-1 or extended sessions — prevents throttling after 15 minutes 1 .
 🔌 Input Power Requirement: True 25W wireless output requires ≥30W USB-C PD input (e.g., 30W or 45W GaN adapter). A 20W wall brick won’t unlock full speed — even with a Qi2.2 pad.
 Pros and Cons: Balanced Assessment
 Who benefits most? 
— Users with iPhone 15 Pro or newer, especially those upgrading from Qi1 pads or relying on slow overnight charging.
— People who keep their phone on a desk or nightstand for ≥4 hours daily.
— Those willing to invest in ecosystem cohesion (case + charger + adapter).
 Who may not benefit — yet? 
— iPhone 14 or older owners: hardware limits max wireless input to 7.5W regardless of charger.
— Frequent travelers: bulkier Qi2.2 stations sacrifice portability.
— Budget-first buyers: certified Qi2.2 starts at $45 — double the cost of reliable Qi1 pads.
 How to Choose an iPhone Wireless Fast Charger
 Follow this 5-step checklist — and avoid these common pitfalls:
 Verify iPhone compatibility: Only iPhone 15 Pro and newer fully support Qi2.2. iPhone 15/16 non-Pro models receive firmware-limited gains (≤18W). Older models get no speed improvement.
 Check for official Qi2.2 certification: Visit the Wireless Power Consortium’s certified products database . Don’t trust retailer badges.
 Confirm magnetic strength and cooling: Look for ≥25 N pull force and either aluminum venting or active fan specs. Avoid “silent” claims — silence often means no active cooling.
 Test your power adapter: Use a 30W+ USB-C PD source. If you’re still using your old 20W brick, upgrade first — it’s the silent bottleneck.
 Avoid these red flags: “Up to 25W” without Qi2.2 logo; no thermal specs listed; no mention of magnetic force; “works with all iPhones” (technically false for pre-15 Pro).
 Insights & Cost Analysis
 Based on verified retail pricing (Q2 2026) and lab-tested performance data:

 Throttles rapidly; no safety guarantees 
 Value insight: The $45–$75 tier delivers >90% of the speed benefit at half the cost of premium stations. Unless you need consolidated charging, pay for performance — not features you won’t use.
 Better Solutions & Competitor Analysis
 Not all Qi2.2 chargers perform equally. Based on thermal imaging, power consistency, and user-reported reliability (aggregated from 12,000+ reviews across CNET, TechGearLab, and Wirecutter), here’s how top-tier models compare:

 Thermal imaging shows Qi2.2-certified units maintain stable coil temps (<42°C); uncertified pads exceed 65°C in under 8 minutes — triggering automatic power reduction. 
 Customer Feedback Synthesis
 Analysis of 8,400+ verified reviews (April–June 2026) reveals consistent patterns:
 Top 3 Compliments: “Charges faster than my old MagSafe,” “Stays cool even after an hour,” “Magnet holds perfectly through my case.”
 Top 3 Complaints: “Fan noise is noticeable in quiet rooms,” “Watch charging is slower than advertised,” “Doesn’t fit well with thick protective cases.”
 Notably, 92% of complaints about speed were traced to one root cause: using a sub-30W power adapter. Once upgraded, satisfaction jumped to 97%.
 Maintenance, Safety & Legal Considerations
 Qi2.2 chargers carry WPC (Wireless Power Consortium) certification — meaning they meet international safety standards for electromagnetic field (EMF) exposure, thermal cutoff, and foreign object detection (FOD). No special maintenance is required beyond occasional dust removal from vents or coil surfaces.
 Important notes:
 Always use a Qi2.2-certified charger with a USB-C PD 3.0 (or higher) power adapter rated ≥30W.
 Avoid placing phones with metal plates, credit cards, or RFID-enabled items between device and charger — FOD systems usually detect them, but risk remains.
 No regulatory body prohibits Qi2.2 use — it complies with FCC Part 18 and IEC 62368-1 standards globally.
 Internal cooling architecture of certified Qi2.2 units — critical for sustaining 25W output without throttling. 
 Conclusion
 If you need real wireless speed and own an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, choose a Qi2.2-certified, magnetically aligned charger with documented thermal management — whether single-pad or 3-in-1. If you want simplicity and value, start with a $45–$75 single pad and a 30W GaN adapter. If you charge multiple Apple devices daily and have desk space, a $99–$129 active-cooled station makes sense. If you own an iPhone 14 or older, wireless fast charging isn’t viable yet — save your budget for a future upgrade. If you’re a typical user, you don’t need to overthink this.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Do I need a new power adapter for Qi2.2 wireless charging? 
 Yes — a minimum 30W USB-C PD adapter is required to unlock full 25W output. Your existing 20W iPhone charger will limit throughput to ~15W, even with a Qi2.2 pad. 
 Will Qi2.2 chargers work with older iPhones? 
 They’ll charge iPhone 12–14 models, but only at legacy Qi1 speeds (≤7.5W). No speed gain occurs without iPhone 15 Pro or newer hardware. 
 Is magnetic alignment really necessary for fast charging? 
 Yes — Qi2.2’s speed depends on precise coil coupling. Without magnets, minor shifts cause immediate power drops and heat buildup. Market data shows 100% of top-performing searches include “magnetic” 
 3 . 
 Can I use a Qi2.2 charger with Android phones? 
 Yes — Qi2.2 is cross-platform. Most Samsung Galaxy S23/S24 and Pixel 8/9 models support it, though maximum speed varies by device (typically 15–20W). 
 Why does my Qi2.2 charger get warm? 
 Some warmth is normal (up to 42°C surface temp), but excessive heat (>50°C) indicates poor ventilation, weak magnets, or insufficient input power. Check your adapter and ensure vents aren’t blocked.

 Apple hasn't announced it yet, but Belkin's new UltraCharge collection seems to confirm that the company is ready to support Qi2.2 (aka Qi2 25W) on third-party chargers. This new standard supports the same 25W wireless charging speeds offered by  the new MagSafe Charger . However, once iOS 26 becomes available, these devices will also support other third-party accessories with Qi2.2.
 According to Belkin's tests, the new UltraCharge collection can charge an iPhone 16 from 0-50% in 25 minutes, which puts wireless charging on par with charging a device with a cable. More importantly, iOS 26 adds other charging features, including a reminder of how long it will take to get to 80% battery and a new Adaptive Power Mode to help your device last longer during the day.
 Of course, users can expect the same benefits when Apple releases the iPhone 17. That said, it's worth noting that MagSafe and Qi2.2 might not become available on the iPhone 17e, as the iPhone 16e lacks some features from the flagship line .

 Apple introduced an updated version of its MagSafe charging puck a year ago that can wirelessly charge its then new iPhone 16 lineup at faster 25W rates. However, when used with other devices, including older iPhone models, charging rates were limited to 15W and slower. A new version of Apple’s MagSafe Charger is now available, and like the iPhone 17 , 17 Pro, and 17 Pro Max , it now fully supports the Qi2.2 standard and can be used to charge other compatible devices (like the Google Pixel 10 Pro XL ) at 25W rates, as spotted by MacRumors and 9to5Mac .
 The new charger, which was first leaked last June through Taiwan’s National Communications Commission’s website, is now available through Apple’s online store with a 1-meter USB-C cable for $39, or a 2-meter cable for $49.
 Apple introduced 25W wireless charging with the iPhone 16 ahead of the Qi2.2 specification being officially introduced early this year, which is why the faster rate was only available when using Apple’s own wireless charger. Now that the iPhone 17 lineup is Qi 2.2 compatible (as will most of the iPhone 16 lineup be once iOS 26 is released ) the phones can be powered up at 25W rates using any wireless charger that supports Qi2.2. However, if you’re upgrading to the iPhone Air, you’re only going to see a maximum of 20W rates when charging wirelessly.

 If you’re looking to declutter your nightstand and quickly charge up to three of your most-used gadgets, Anker’s Prime Wireless Charging Station is an easy way to do both. The station has spots for your MagSafe-ready iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods, and right now it’s down to a new all-time low of $134.99 ($95 off) in white at Amazon and directly from Anker with code WS7DV2LJ3JGU . You can also buy it in black from either retailer for $5 more.

 $ 135 $ 230 41 % off 
 $ 135 
 $135 at Amazon $135 at Anker (with code WS7DV2LJ3JGU) 
 The Qi2.2-compatible charger supports up to 25W wireless charging for compatible iPhones (the iPhone 16 and up, excluding the 16E and 17E). Anker claims this charging station can bring an iPhone 17 Pro from 0 to 50 percent in about 22 minutes. It also includes dedicated 5W charging pads for an Apple Watch and AirPods (or another pair that includes a wireless charging case), allowing you to power all three devices simultaneously. You can switch between three charging modes depending on your priorities, whether that’s fast top-ups, cooler charging, or quiet, slower charging overnight.

 What makes this 3-in-1 charger stand out from the competition is its 1.65-inch touchscreen that displays each device’s charging status, power draw, or temperature. If you’d rather customize things, you can pair it with Anker’s app to adjust settings, switch charging modes, and tweak the display. The adjustable phone stand tilts up to 80 degrees, and Anker even includes a 65W USB-C power adapter and cable in the box, so you won’t need to buy those separately.

It also features a bright 1.47-inch color display, and supports measurements in six different units. The digital tape measure can calculate distance, area, and volume, too. It supports USB-C charging and stores up to 30 previous measurements. Sounds like a good upgrade to me if you’re always tinkering. 
 You can save up to $700 on LG’s C6 series of OLED TVs when you buy directly from LG , with free installation and up to $200 in Uber Eats or DoorDash credits that you won’t get from other retailers. All of the TVs in this series sport excellent OLED panels with rich contrast and deep blacks, along with support for 165Hz refresh rate, Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium variable refresh rate, Dolby Atmos support, and more.

 Apple introduced its iPhone 17 range at yesterday’s Awe Dropping event 
 Plenty of new features were revealed during the show 
 But there were several important changes that got no airtime 
 Apple ’s ‘Awe Dropping’ event saw the release of the new iPhone 17 range , plus the radically slimline iPhone Air .
 But while Apple spilled the beans on almost every aspect of these devices, there were still plenty of details it didn’t announce on stage - here are some of the most interesting but hidden new features in the iPhone 17 lineup.
 Faster charging…
 Alongside the iPhone 17, Apple has also launched a new 'Dynamic' power adapter that costs $39. It’s rated for 40W of power delivery, but it can dynamically ramp up to 60W in short bursts. This enables the iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max to be powered up to 50% in around 20 minutes – an improvement over the 30 minutes you’ll get with the iPhone 16 series.
 Latest Videos From TechRadar 
 Watch full video here: 
 The iPhone 17 devices also support 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging , meaning you won’t need a MagSafe charger to hit these speeds – any compatible third-party accessory can now achieve these rates as well.
 …but not for the iPhone Air
 (Image credit: Apple) Although the advancements above apply to the iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, the iPhone Air unfortunately misses out. For one thing, it’s limited to 20W MagSafe and Qi2 charging rates instead of the 25W you’ll get with all other models.
 You may like
 15 things we learned from Apple's big iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro launch 
 iPhone 17 Pro vs iPhone 18 Pro: 5 key differences between Apple's best 
 Apple Event 2026 recap — foldable iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, AirPods 5, and more 
 As well as that, the iPhone Air’s fast-charging speeds are slower than those of its siblings: you’ll hit 50% after 30 minutes, not 20 minutes.
 The return of the MagSafe Battery
 The MagSafe Battery magnetically snaps to your iPhone in order to wirelessly juice it up. This accessory only works magnetically with the iPhone Air, however, as the camera bumps of the iPhone 17 models get in the way, meaning they’re not compatible.
 Get daily insight, inspiration and deals in your inbox
 Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
 That said, the MagSafe Battery is technically compatible with other devices. While the iPhone Air is the only iPhone it works with, Apple says it can be used to “charge smaller accessories via USB-C.” Apple didn’t specify which accessories it works with, but we expect it should be able to act as a battery pack and power up any device that charges over USB-C.
 Thwarting spyware and hackers
 (Image credit: Lance Ulanoff / Future) Apple is hot on security, and that continues in the iPhone 17 lineup. In a blog post , Apple explained how these phones come with a feature called Memory Integrity Enforcement (MIE), which is designed to protect against memory corruption exploits.
 These vulnerabilities are frequently used by high-end spyware that’s used on a nation-state level. While that means most iOS users won’t be targeted, some most definitely will. To put a stop to that, Apple’s MIE adds hidden tags to every memory block in the iPhone. If something wants to use that memory but doesn’t match the hidden tag, it will be blocked, significantly raising the costs of successful spyware techniques and keeping your iPhone safer than ever.
 What to read next
 5 biggest iPhone 18 rumors rated — what to really expect at next week's Apple event 
 Apple iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max review: better in all the right places 
 iPhone 18 Pro vs iPhone 17: which should you choose? 
 A fix for screen flickering
 Apple uses pulse width modulation (PWM) to control the brightness of your iPhone, and it works by quickly flickering LED or OLED pixels on and off. This causes discomfort for some users in the form of headaches and eye strain, but the iPhone 17 Pro has a way to fix it.
 This iPhone has an accessibility setting that lets you disable PWM if you want to. According to MacRumors , it’s only been spotted in the iPhone 17 Pro so far, but it might be extended to other devices in the range.
 Feeling the heat
 (Image credit: Lance Ulanoff / Future) You may have noticed that the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max have ditched the titanium frames that last year’s phones possessed and have instead switched to aluminum. Apple mentioned the change at its event, but it didn’t give a reason.
 The most likely cause is heat dissipation. Aluminum is far more heat conductive than titanium, meaning it can disperse high temperatures much more quickly and efficiently. Combined with the new vapor chamber in the iPhone 17 Pro devices, that should help them keep cooler than ever when running the powerful new A19 Pro chips.
 FineWoven isn’t dead yet
 Apple’s FineWoven cases caused a stir when they launched with the iPhone 15 series, and not in a good way, as the products were prone to scuffs and discoloration that rapidly degraded their look and feel. But although Apple hasn’t launched any new FineWoven cases – and seems to have replaced them with a new TechWoven alternative – FineWoven lives on.
 It didn’t get any airtime at the iPhone 17 event, but Apple has launched a new set of MagSafe wallets and AirTag key rings made from FineWoven, suggesting that reports of the material’s death have been greatly exaggerated.
 No mmWave for all
 (Image credit: Apple) Apple proudly showed off its C1X chip at the iPhone 17 event, and this modem powers the 5G connectivity every new iPhone comes with. But there was one drawback that Apple forgot to mention.
 That’s the fact that the iPhone Air loses out on mmWave functionality. The C1X includes mmWave in the iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, and iPhone 17 Pro Max, and this offers faster speeds compared to regular 5G, but Apple’s thinnest and lightest phone misses out.
 Two-tier transfer rates
 Want the fastest transfer speeds when sending files over USB-C? You’ll want to stick to the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max. While these devices offer USB 3 speeds of up to 10Gbps, the iPhone 17 and iPhone Air are far more restrictive.
 That’s because they’re limited to USB 2 speeds, which top out at 480Mbps. That’ll result in far slower transfer speeds when you’re using a cable.

e The iPhone 17 is a smartphone developed and marketed by Apple that is part of the nineteenth generation of the iPhone . Succeeding the iPhone 16 series, the device was announced alongside the higher-priced, refreshed iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max and the new iPhone Air during an Apple Event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California , on September 9, 2025. History [ edit | edit source ] The device was announced alongside the higher-priced, refreshed iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max and the new iPhone Air during an Apple Event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California , on September 9, 2025, [ 3 ] and released on September 19. [ 4 ] In a break with the iPhone Plus product line that had existed for the previous three generations, Apple did not unveil an iPhone 17 Plus. [ 5 ] [ 6 ] Its role in the product lineup was replaced by the new iPhone Air, which represented a strategic shift to a lighter, thinner product. [ 5 ] Design [ edit | edit source ] iPhone 17 phones in each different color The iPhone 17 comes in five colors: Lavender, Sage, Mist Blue, White, and Black. [ 7 ] Compared to the previous model (the iPhone 16 ), the iPhone 17 uses the same design while improving internal hardware and shrinking the display bezels. Furthermore, the display is larger at 6.3   in (160   mm) , compared to the previous model's 6.1   in (150   mm) . [ 8 ] Color Name Lavender Sage Mist Blue White Black Specifications [ edit | edit source ] Chipset [ edit | edit source ] The iPhone 17 uses the Apple A19 chip. It incorporates the Apple-designed N1 networking chip, part of a trend by Apple to reduce reliance on Broadcom and third-party chip suppliers. [ 9 ] The N1 supports Wi-Fi 7 , Bluetooth 6.0 , and Thread . The iPhone 17 does not use Apple's new C1X modem found in the iPhone Air, opting instead for Qualcomm 's Snapdragon X80 . [ 10 ] Apple said it intends to continue adoption of its own chips going forward, but that was not the focus for this year. [ 11 ] The iPhone 17 also removes the 128   GB storage option available on its predecessor, the iPhone 16 , making the base model iPhone the first to come only with 256   GB and 512   GB of storage. At launch, prices started at US$799, [ 12 ] before being raised to US$899 on September 9, 2026. [ 13 ] Display [ edit | edit source ] The iPhone 17 has a 6.3-inch (160   mm) LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED display with a resolution of 2622 × 1206 at 460 pixels per inch . It supports a dynamic refresh rate of up to 120   Hz through ProMotion, the first time the technology was included on a non-Pro iPhone model. [ 3 ] The display supports HDR10 , always-on display , True Tone, P3 wide color , and Haptic Touch , and incorporates the Dynamic Island . It has a 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio. Its brightness ranges from 1   nit to 1,000   nits typical brightness, 1,600   nits peak brightness for HDR content, and 3,000   nits peak outdoor brightness. The display is protected by Ceramic Shield 2, which Apple claims provides three times the scratch resistance of the previous generation, and has fingerprint-resistant oleophobic and anti-reflective coatings. [ 14 ] Camera [ edit | edit source ] The iPhone 17 uses a 48-megapixel Dual Fusion camera system, with a 48-megapixel Fusion main lens, and a 48   MP Fusion ultra-wide. This enables 12   MP shots with zoom up to 2x with optical quality using the main camera lens. The front camera uses an 18   MP Center Stage camera with Dual Capture, which allows it to be used in any orientation and to create either a landscape or portrait photo, based on who is in the shot. [ 14 ] Security [ edit | edit source ] Starting with all iPhone 17 models and iPhone Air , devices based on the A19 and A19 Pro include Memory Integrity Enforcement (MIE). [ 15 ] [ 16 ] MIE is an always-on, hardware-and-OS, memory-safety defense that uses Apple's secure memory allocators, Enhanced Memory Tagging Extension (EMTE) in synchronous mode, and Tag Confidentiality Enforcement policies. [ 15 ] By default, MIE hardens key attack surfaces, including the kernel and over 70 userland processes, while preserving performance. [ 15 ] Apple states that MIE targets mercenary spyware by making end-to-end exploit chains significantly more expensive and difficult to develop and maintain. [ 15 ] Comparison of iPhone 16 and iPhone 17 specifications Feature iPhone 16 iPhone 17 Display size 6.1-inch 6.3-inch Display technology 60 Hz ProMotion (120 Hz) with Always-On Display Front glass Ceramic Shield Ceramic Shield 2 Processor Apple A18 Apple A19 Front camera 12 MP TrueDepth 18 MP Center Stage Ultrawide camera 12 MP 48 MP Camera features Standard capture Tap to zoom and rotate, Center Stage for photos/video calls, Dual capture Video stabilization Cinematic video stabilization Ultra-stabilized video Battery life Up to 22 hours video playback Up to 30 hours video playback Wireless charging MagSafe (Up to 22W ) MagSafe (Up to 25W) [ 17 ] Reception [ edit | edit source ] IGN 's Shubham Agarwal described the iPhone 17 as "Apple's best entry-level iPhone in years", praising the 120   Hz display and the faster 40   W charging for the first time in a non-Pro iPhone model, but criticizing its camera quality in low-light conditions. [ 18 ] The A19 was praised for its performance in day-to-day use and multitasking , though IGN noted that "[g]aming performance isn’t as strong as the Pro's, and though it can smoothly run the majority of games on the App Store , some of the heavier ones, like Assassin's Creed Mirage , can stutter at the highest graphic settings." [ 18 ] Release [ edit | edit source ] Pre-orders for the iPhone 17 began on September 12, 2025, and they became available on September 19, 2025. MagSafe (wireless charger) - Wikipedia 
 Jump to content 
 From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
 Magnetic connection system for Apple products
 For the wired magnetic power connector used in MacBook, see MagSafe .
 MagSafe 
 MagSafe Charger
 Type 
 Smartphone wireless charging connector 
 Production history 
 Designer 
 Apple Inc. 
 Manufacturer 
Apple Inc. 
 Produced 
October 2020 (6 years ago)   ( October 2020 ) 
 Hot pluggable 
Yes 
 External 
Yes 
 MagSafe is a proprietary , magnetically attached wireless power transfer and accessory-attachment standard developed by Apple Inc. for its iPhone and AirPods product lines. It was announced on October 13, 2020, in conjunction with the iPhone 12 and 12 Pro series. 
 The first version of MagSafe provides up to 15   W of power and is compatible with the open Qi standard for up to 7.5   W of power. The second version, announced in 2024 in conjunction with the iPhone 16 and 16 Pro , provides up to 25   W of power and is compatible with the Qi2 standard for up to 15   W of power. A revised MagSafe Charger released in 2025 supports Qi2 charging up to 25   W. The connector also enables connecting non-charger accessories such as card holders and cases with communication through an integrated NFC loop. The charger uses a circle of rare-earth magnets . [ 1 ] 
 Apple released two chargers using the MagSafe standard in 2020: the MagSafe Charger, which is a single charging pad for iPhone, and the MagSafe Duo Charger, which is a charging mat with both MagSafe and an Apple Watch charger. [ 2 ] Apple has also licensed the MagSafe standard to third parties to develop chargers and cases. In 2021, Apple released the MagSafe Battery Pack and added MagSafe charging to AirPods and AirPods Pro . In 2025, Apple released a MagSafe Battery exclusively for the iPhone Air .
 History
 [ edit ] 
 The MagSafe name was first used by Apple for the conductive power connectors of its MacBook lineup, beginning with the 2006 MacBook Pro . It began to be phased out upon the release of the 2015 MacBook, which used USB Power Delivery and the USB-C connector for charging. [ 3 ] MagSafe was discontinued across MacBooks in 2019 but reintroduced with 14   in (360   mm) and 16   in (410   mm) MacBook Pro models released in October 2021. [ 4 ] 
 In 2017, Apple announced AirPower , a wireless charging mat capable of charging an iPhone, AirPods and Apple Watch (which uses a proprietary wireless charging system) simultaneously and the devices could be placed anywhere on the mat. However, it was canceled in early 2019 due to overheating issues caused by the many overlapping coils.
 Apple announced MagSafe along with the iPhone 12 series on October 13, 2020, during the “Hi, Speed” Apple Special Event as a universal ecosystem of wireless charging and accessories. Apple's chargers based on MagSafe are their first to use the Qi standard , following the development of AirPower. [ 5 ] The MagSafe receptacle on iPhones, internally called MagSafe Attach, [ 6 ] uses magnets to align automatically and attach to a Qi charger, ensuring reliable charging. [ 7 ] [ 8 ] 
 On October 18, 2021, Apple released the 3rd generation AirPods and an updated SKU of AirPods Pro with a bundled MagSafe charging case. [ 9 ] 
 In 2023, the Wireless Power Consortium announced the Qi2 standard that is based on MagSafe. [ 10 ] 
 Chargers and accessories
 [ edit ] 
 MagSafe Charger
 [ edit ] 
 The MagSafe Charger is a single charging pad that contains recyclable rare-earth magnets surrounding a Qi wireless charging coil with a 1   m cable terminating in a USB‑C plug. The first version of the MagSafe Charger, released in 2020, delivers up to 15   W of power to iPhones 12, 12 Pro, and newer, with the exception of iPhone 12 Mini and 13 Mini, which support 12   W. [ 11 ] The Wall Street Journal found the MagSafe Charger charged at half the speed of a 20   W wired charger. [ 12 ] Being a Qi charger, the MagSafe Charger can charge all Qi-certified devices, including older iPhone models and AirPods, though testing by MacRumors found that MagSafe charged iPhones older than the 12 series at around half the speed of third-party 7.5   W Qi chargers. [ 13 ] Devices without MagSafe or Qi2's Magnetic Power Profile (MPP) need to be manually aligned as they do not have the built-in array of magnets that interlock with MagSafe. [ 14 ] [ 15 ] Apple recommends a 20   W power adapter. [ 16 ] Users have reported MagSafe Chargers leaving circular imprints on leather cases. [ 17 ] 
 On September 9, 2024, Apple discontinued the original MagSafe Charger and replaced it with a second-generation model that provides up to 25   W charging with the iPhone 16 / 16 Pro series and newer, and 20   W with the iPhone Air . It is compatible with the Qi2 standard for up to 15   W of power. Apple recommends a 30   W power adapter. [ 18 ] In September 2025, Apple released an updated version with support for 25   W Qi2 charging. [ 19 ] 
 MagSafe Duo Charger
 [ edit ] 
 The MagSafe Duo Charger is a foldable charging mat with a MagSafe charger on one side and an Apple Watch charger on the other. The Apple Watch charger disc can be laid flat for face-up charging or can be vertical for nightstand use. The MagSafe Duo charger can be folded when not in use. [ 20 ] [ 21 ] The charger came with a Lightning–to–USB-C cable, and Apple recommends their newer 30 W USB-C power adapter (released in 2018), and notes their older 29 W adapter is incompatible and can only charge one device at a time. [ 22 ] 
 Durability testing performed by Apple Insider found that the hinge could fail with frequent folding, noting it "started to break down at 180 folds and ultimately failed at 212." [ 23 ] The larger camera array on the iPhone 13 Pro and later models elevates the top end from the charger with a case so it not longer sits flush, though charging is unaffected. [ 24 ] The MagSafe Duo does not support fast charging on Apple Watches released since 2021 ( Series 7 and later, Ultra ). [ 25 ] The MagSafe Duo was discontinued in September 2023. [ 26 ] 
 MagSafe Battery Pack
 [ edit ] 
 In July 2021, Apple released the MagSafe Battery Pack (A2384). It contains a 11.13   W⋅h, 1,460   mA⋅h battery that on its own can charge an iPhone at up to 7.5   W. [ 27 ] While the pack is being charged via Lightning it can charge an iPhone at up to 15   W. The pack itself can be charged either directly through its Lightning port or wirelessly from an iPhone that is being charged via Lightning (ie Reverse wireless charging ). [ 28 ] [ 29 ] [ 30 ] Height 95.8 mm, width 64.13 mm, thickness 11.28 mm and weight of 113.8 grams. [ 31 ] The MagSafe Battery Pack was discontinued in September 2023 after the iPhone 15 series was released, which charges via USB‑C for wired charging rather than Lightning. [ 26 ] 
 MagSafe Battery for iPhone Air
 [ edit ] 
 On September 9, 2025, Apple released the MagSafe Battery which is only compatible with the iPhone Air (A3466) and provides up to an extra 65% charge. It supports 12 W wireless charging, or up to 20 W when connected to a power adapter. It can also be reversed charged by an iPhone connected to power. It can charge smaller accessories using its USB-C port at up to 4.5 W. [ 32 ] [ 33 ] It will function with other iPhones and devices with MagSafe and/or Qi, but the camera bumps on other iPhones prevent it from sitting flat, it will only mount flush when sideways. [ 34 ] 3149 mAh, 12.26 Wh, input 5-9V 3A, output 5V 1.5A PD 3.0 , certified CE and CCC. Height 122.24 mm, width 70.78 mm, thickness 7.72 mm and weight of 126.5 grams. [ 35 ] 
 Cases, wallets and sleeves
 [ edit ] 
 A clear iPhone case showing the MagSafe magnet layout 
 Apple released a line of MagSafe cases and other accessories, such as leather sleeves and wallets that can attach magnetically to iPhones and cases with MagSafe. Apple states MagSafe charging works through their cases. Apple states that their leather wallets are shielded to protect credit cards from the rare-earth magnets used in these accessories, although warns that credit cards should not be placed between an iPhone and a MagSafe charger. [ 36 ] In 2021, Apple released an updated MagSafe wallet with an NFC chip that supports Find My location tracking when the wallet is disconnected from an iPhone, but is not supported by Apple's clear cases for iPhone 12 models. [ 37 ] In 2023, with the iPhone 15 family, Apple replaced the leather MagSafe wallet with a FineWoven version. [ 38 ] [ 39 ] The FineWoven cases were replaced with "TechWoven" cases in 2025 with the iPhone 17 family. [ 40 ] 
 Third-party chargers and accessories
 [ edit ] 
 Apple refers to officially licensed third-party MagSafe products as " Made for MagSafe ". Apple worked with Belkin to design chargers using MagSafe. [ 41 ] [ 42 ] At launch, Belkin was the only accessory maker to which Apple had licensed the MagSafe charging standard; while other third-party accessory makers advertise magnetic charging products as "MagSafe compatible," they use older Qi standards that deliver a maximum charging speed of 7.5   W, compared to first-generation MagSafe's 15   W, and lack integrated NFC . [ 43 ] [ 44 ] In 2022, accessory maker Mophie worked with Apple to release a 3-in-1 Made for MagSafe travel charger; Nomad also released a charging base. [ 45 ] [ 46 ] OtterBox manufactures officially licensed cases and a 2-in-1 charger. [ 47 ] [ 48 ] 
 Devices supporting MagSafe
 [ edit ] 
 The following devices support MagSafe:
 iPhones released in October 2020 and later ( iPhone 12 / 12 Pro and newer) except the iPhone SE (3rd generation) and iPhone 16e 
 The iPhone 16 / 16 Pro and newer support 25 W charging with the second-generation MagSafe Charger, with the exception of the iPhone Air which supports 20 W charging, and the iPhone 17e which supports 15 W charging. The iPhone 12/12 Pro and newer (except the 3rd generation iPhone SE and iPhone 16e) support Qi2 with iOS 17.4 . [ 49 ] 
 MagSafe Charging Case for AirPods (3rd generation)
 The wireless charging case for AirPods (4th generation) does not have magnets to automatically align with MagSafe chargers due to its smaller size.
 MagSafe Charging Case for AirPods Pro (first-generation SKUs after October 2021, and second generation and newer)
 MagSafe compatible
 [ edit ] 
 See also: Qi2 25W 
 MagSafe chargers are listed as compatible with all iPhones with Qi charging , which includes the iPhone   8 through iPhone   11 family; however, the magnetic function cannot be used and only charging up to 7.5   W is supported. MagSafe cases or stickers for those phones are not MFi-certified and may interfere with the compass and GPS. [ 50 ] [ 51 ]

Previous versions: Open standard Copyright Logo and trademark Website chargewithqi .com Qi ( / tʃ iː / CHEE ) is an open standard for inductive charging developed by the Wireless Power Consortium . It allows compatible devices, such as smartphones , to receive power when placed on a Qi charger, which can be effective over distances up to 4   cm (1.6   in). [ 1 ] Devices that implement the optional Magnetic Power Profile, based on Apple's MagSafe wireless charging technology, using magnets for better device attachment and alignment to a charger may be labelled Qi2. [ 2 ] Qi version 1.0 was released in 2010; by 2017, it had been incorporated into more than 200 models of smartphones, tablets, and other devices. [ 3 ] In December 2023, 351 manufacturers were working with the standard, including Apple , Asus , Google , Huawei , LG Electronics , Samsung , Xiaomi , and Sony . [ 4 ] The Qi specification version 2.2, released in April 2025, supports charging speeds of up to 25 watts and aims to improve compatibility across devices from various manufacturers. [ 5 ] [ 6 ] The current version 2.2.1 released in July 2025 includes Qi2 25   W branding for the 25-watt charging mode. [ 7 ] Naming [ edit ] The name of the Qi standard comes from the Mandarin qì ( simplified Chinese : 气 ; traditional Chinese : 氣 ), meaning "life force" or "vital energy". [ 8 ] [ 9 ] Design [ edit ] Fig. 1-1 Devices that operate using the Qi standard rely on electromagnetic induction between planar coils . A Qi system consists of two types of devices – the Base Station, which is connected to a power source and provides inductive power, and Mobile Devices, which consume inductive power. The Base Station contains a power transmitter that comprises a transmitting coil that generates an oscillating magnetic field ; the Mobile Device contains a power receiver holding a receiving coil. The magnetic field induces an alternating current in the receiving coil by Faraday's law of induction . Close spacing of the two coils ensures the inductive power transfer is efficient. [ citation needed ] Base Stations typically have a flat surface – referred to as the Interface Surface – on top of which a user can place one or more Mobile Devices. There are two methods for aligning the transmitting coil (part of the Base Station) and receiving coil (part of the Mobile Device) in order for a power transfer to happen. In the first concept – called guided positioning – a user must place the Mobile Device on a certain location of the Base Station's surface. For this purpose, the Mobile Device provides an alignment aid that is appropriate to its size, shape, and function. The second concept – referred to as free positioning – does not require the user to place the Mobile Device in direct alignment with the transmitting coil. There are several ways to achieve free positioning. In one example a bundle of transmitting coils is used to generate a magnetic field at the location of the receiving coil only. Another example uses mechanical means to move a single transmitting coil underneath the receiving coil. A third option is to use a technique called Multiple Cooperative Flux Generators . [ 10 ] The power transmitter includes a power conversion unit and a communications and control unit. Figure 1-1 shows the transmitting coil (array) generating the magnetic field as part of the power conversion unit. The control and communications unit regulates the transferred power to the level that the power receiver requests. A Base Station may contain numerous transmitters, allowing for multiple Mobile Devices to be placed on the same Base Station to charge each of its batteries. [ citation needed ] A power receiver comprises a power pick-up unit, and a communications and control unit. A power pick-up unit typically contains a single receiving coil only. The mobile device it charges typically contains a single power receiver. The communications and control unit regulates the transferred power to the level that is appropriate for the device. [ citation needed ] Transmitters [ edit ] A reference Qi low-power transmitter has a coil of 20 turns (in two layers) in a flat coil, wound on a form with a 19   mm inner diameter and a 40   mm outer diameter, with a below-coil shield of soft iron at least 4   mm larger in diameter, which gives an inductance of 24   ±   1 microhenries. This coil is placed in a series resonant circuit that is driven by an H-bridge switching arrangement from the DC source. Power control is automatic and voltage is controllable in steps of 50 millivolts or less. [ citation needed ] In the device a proportional–integral–derivative controller is used to modulate the delivered power according to the primary cell voltage. [ citation needed ] Other Qi charge transmitters start their connections at 140   kHz, but can adjust to find a frequency to better match the distance between coils. Different Qi reference designs have different coil arrangements, including oval coil and multi-coil systems as well as more complex resonance networks with multiple inductors and capacitors. These designs allow operation at frequencies from 105 to 205   kHz and with maximum resonant circuit voltages as high as 200 volts. [ citation needed ] Receivers [ edit ] The Qi power receiver hardware reference design starts with a rectangular coil of wire 44   mm × 30   mm outside size, with 14 turns of wire, and with an above-coil magnetic shield. [ citation needed ] Power output to the portable device is via a full-wave bridge ; the power is typically filtered with a capacitor before delivery to the charge controller. [ citation needed ] Other Qi power receivers use alternate resonance modulators, including switching a resistor or pair of resistors across the receiver resonator capacitor, both before and after the bridge rectifier. [ citation needed ] Features and specifications [ edit ] See also: Wireless Power Consortium §   Introduction of Wireless Standards The bottom side of an LG WCP-300 Qi charging pad Opened Nokia DT-900 Qi charger The Wireless Power Consortium (WPC) published the Qi low-power specification in August 2009. [ 11 ] The Qi specification can be downloaded freely after registration. [ 12 ] Under the Qi specification, "low power" inductive transfers deliver power below 5   W using inductive coupling between two planar coils . These coils are typically 5   mm apart but can be up to 40   mm and possibly further apart. [ 13 ] The Qi low-power specification has been renamed to the Qi Baseline Power Profile. [ 14 ] Regulation of the output voltage is provided by a digital control loop where the power receiver communicates with the power transmitter and requests more or less power. Communication is unidirectional from the power receiver to the power transmitter via backscatter modulation. In backscatter modulation, the power-receiver coil is loaded, changing the current draw at the power transmitter. These current changes are monitored and demodulated into the information required for the two devices to work together. [ 1 ] In 2011, the WPC began to extend the Qi specification to medium power. [ 15 ] As of 2019, the Medium Power standard currently delivers 30 to 65   W. It is expected to eventually support up to 200   W (typically used for portable power tools, robotic vacuum cleaners, drones and e-bikes). [ 16 ] In 2015, the WPC also demonstrated a high-power specification, called "Ki", that will deliver up to 1   kW, allowing the powering of kitchen appliances among other high-power utilities. [ 12 ] In 2015, WPC introduced the Qi Extended Power Profile specification, which supports charging phones at up to 15   W. Phone companies that support this include LG , Sony , Xiaomi , and Sharp . [ 17 ] [ 18 ] [ 19 ] [ 20 ] In 2024, WPC upgraded Ki to support 2.2   kW wireless power delivery. [ 21 ] [ 22 ] WPC introduced Proprietary Power Delivery Extension to allow phone OEMs to deliver higher than Baseline Power Profile's 5   W or the Extended Power Profile's 15   W. Currently, only Samsung has published their compliance test. [ 23 ] Other phone companies that use proprietary standards for fast wireless charging include Apple, Huawei and Google. [ citation needed ] With Qi version 2.0, WPC introduced Magnetic Power Profile (MPP), an optional part of the specification based on Apple's MagSafe for iPhone . This enables magnetic attachment and alignment with a ring of permanent magnets around the charging coil and is backwards compatible with MagSafe devices. Devices that implement MPP use a new logo and branding, Qi2 in a circle, to distinguish them from Qi devices that do not support MPP (even if they otherwise support Qi v2.0 or later). [ 24 ] The "Qi2 in a circle" logo has previously been sporadically used for Qi2 without MPP, this usage is officially disapproved for new products. Previously Qi(1) products are to be labeled as Qi2, as use of the Qi(1) logo has been discontinued. [ 25 ] Adoption [ edit ] Nokia first adopted Qi in its Lumia 920 , and Samsung Mobile on the Galaxy S3 (supported via a retrofittable official Samsung back cover accessory) in 2012, [ 26 ] the Google/LG Nexus 4 followed later that year. Toyota began offering a Qi charging cradle as a factory option on its 2013 Avalon Limited , [ 27 ] with Ssangyong the second car manufacturer to offer a Qi option, also in 2013. [ 28 ] As the Qi standard gained popularity, Qi Hotspots began to arise in places such as coffee shops, airports, sports arenas, etc. [ 29 ] In 2012, The Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf , a US coffee chain, announced plans to install inductive charging stations at selected major metropolitan cities, [ 30 ] as did Virgin Atlantic , for United Kingdom's London Heathrow Airport , [ 31 ] and New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport . [ 32 ] In 2015, a survey found that 76% of people surveyed in the United States and China were aware of wireless charging (an increase from 36% the previous year), and 16% of those were using it daily. [ 33 ] Furniture retailer IKEA introduced lamps and tables with integrated wireless chargers for sale in 2015, [ 34 ] and the Lexus NX gained an optional Qi charging pad in the center console. [ 35 ] An estimated 120 million wirelessly charging phones were sold that year, [ 33 ] notably the Samsung Galaxy S6 , which supported both Qi and the competing Power Matters Alliance standards. [ 36 ] By early 2017, Qi had displaced other competing standards such as Rezence . [ 37 ] On September 12, 2017, Apple announced that their new smartphones, the iPhone 8 , iPhone 8 Plus, and the iPhone X , would support the Qi standard. Since then, every new iPhone version has supported the Qi wireless charging standard. [ 38 ] Apple also announced plans to expand the standard with a new protocol called AirPower , which would have added the ability to charge multiple devices at once; however, this was canceled on March 29, 2019. [ 39 ] By the initial launch of iOS 17 in 2023, Apple launched the iPhone 15 models and iPhone 15 Pro models to support the fast 15   W Qi2-certified wireless charging. [ 40 ] [ 41 ] With iOS 17.2, Apple added the fast 15   W Qi2-certified wireless charging support for the iPhone 13 models, iPhone 13 Pro models, iPhone 14 models and iPhone 14 Pro models. [ 42 ] In July 2024, HMD Global announced the Skyline, which became the first Android device to support the Qi2 MPP standard. [ 43 ] [ 44 ] On September 9, 2024, alongside the announcement of the iPhone 16 models and iPhone 16 Pro models, Apple launched a new 25   W MagSafe charger featuring a woven braided cable design, available in 1   m and 2   m length options and maintaining the compatibility with the 15   W Qi2-certified wireless charging standard. [ 45 ] [ 46 ] In January 2025, Samsung announced that their latest Galaxy S25 series phones are "Qi2 ready". This means that while the devices themselves do not have magnets built-in, they are fully compatible with Qi2 when paired with a magnetic case. [ 47 ] In August 2025, the Google Pixel 10 range became the first major Android phones to include built-in magnets for Qi2 MPP. [ 48 ] The Google Pixel 10 Pro XL also became the first device to support the new Qi2 25   W standard. [ 49 ] Version history [ edit ] Qi versions [ 50 ] Version number Released [ 50 ] Maximum power Notes 1.0 July 2010 5 W Power transmitter can be a single coil, coil array, or moving coil 1.1 March 2012 5 W 12 different transmitter specifications, foreign object detection to prevent heating of metal objects near transmitter, added powering transmitter over USB 1.2 October 2015 Baseline Power Profile: 5   W Extended Power Profile: 15   W Increased maximum transmitter power to 15   W, improved thermal tests for transmitters, improved timing specs, improved foreign object detection sensitivity, optional receiver ID (WP-ID). Labeled by Samsung as "Fast Wireless Charging" (initially 10   W, introduced on the Galaxy Note 5 and S6 edge plus , August 2015) requires charging plate to be connected to Qualcomm Quick Charge 2.0-enabled 15   W USB charger (9   V, 1.67   A support). 1.2.3 February 2017 Extended Power Profile Class 0: 5–30   W Added Power Class 0, which allows the consumer to negotiate up to 30   W from the charger [ 51 ] 1.3 January 2021 Completely restructured Specification documents with 15 thematic books describing different aspects of the system Support for authentication of Qi Certified wireless chargers Improved foreign object detection features and testing (including a new low-Q test power receiver) Restrictions on the negotiable power levels Resolution of mistakes, inconsistencies, and ambiguities A substantial number of new compliance tests covering the new features as well as features that were not tested in older version of the specification 2.0 April 2023 15 W [ 52 ] Incorporates Apple's MagSafe standard for alignment and mounting. Rather than requiring the user to manually align the coils through trial and error while looking for an indication of charging, it aligns the device and charging coil automatically, and also provides for mounting small devices, e.g. phones, securely enough for stationary use, or both. Initial standard supports up to 15   W power, but higher power profiles are planned. Also referred to as Qi2, and certified products may display a Qi2 logo. 2.1 September 2024 Support for Automatic Alignment Profile (AAP) Power Transmitters Support for Magnetic Accessory Covers – MCPE and MCPM Profiles Updated Power Profile and Feature definitions Updated tests to resolve smartphone camera bump mechanical interference with wireless charger Error corrections 2.2 April 2025 25 W Support for up to 25 watt power transfer Power modes optimizing the power transfer to the capabilities of (USB-C) power adapters Gain measurement and gain linearization to optimize the power control Re-introducing capacitive modulation for power receiver communications Improved magnetic power loss accounting Mated Q-factor check to verify absence of foreign object before starting the power transfer Power loss calibration for foreign object detection above 15-watt power levels 2.2.1 July 2025 Introduced Qi2 25   W branding for 25-watt devices and chargers 2.3 December 2025 System gain change reporting for a power transmitter. results.title: The 7 Best iPhone Chargers for Keeping Your Phone Juiced
results.snippet: This guide explains how to choose an iPhone charger based on charging speed, device compatibility, and intended use. Newer models require increasingly powerful equipment: the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max can reach 50 percent in about 15 minutes with a 60-watt USB-C Power Delivery adapter supporting AVS, while the iPhone 17 needs roughly 40 watts and the iPhone 15 and 16 need about 20 watts. Wireless charging reaches up to 25 watts on iPhone 16 and later through MagSafe or Qi2, while the iPhone 15 is limited to 15 watts. Recommended products include Apple’s adaptive 60-watt adapter, compact Anker

 What to Consider 
 The beauty of getting a new iPhone is that it typically offers faster charging than the one it replaced, especially if yours is a few years old. With the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max now leading Apple’s lineup , a 60-watt-capable adapter takes the 18 Pro from empty to 50 percent in about 15 minutes, and wireless charging tops out at 25 watts over MagSafe. Every iPhone Apple sells now uses USB-C , so unless you’re holding an iPhone 14 or older, the Lightning cables in your drawer can stay there.
 The Best iPhone Chargers
 Best Overall : Apple 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with 60W Max ​
 Best Budget : Anker Nano Charger (30W) ​
 Best Smart Display Charger : Anker Nano Charger (45W) ​
 Best for Charging Multiple Devices : Anker 100W USB-C Charger (3-Port, Smart Display) ​
 Best Nightstand Charger : Belkin Qi2.2 25W 3-in-1 Charging Station ​
 To hit full speed, you need a USB-C wall adapter that can deliver the wattage and a cable rated to carry it. For the 18 Pro, that means a 60-watt-capable adapter or higher with Adjustable Voltage Supply. On the other hand, the iPhone 15 and 16 reach 50 percent in about 30 minutes on a 20-watt adapter, and the iPhone 17 does it in about 20 minutes on a 40-watt one. If you’d rather skip cords, a Qi2 or MagSafe pad with a 30-watt adapter gets you the 25-watt wireless speed, though the iPhone 15 caps at 15 watts. Get the combination of wall adapter and cable wrong and your phone will charge at a fraction of what it’s capable of.
 Below are the chargers, cables, docks, and power banks worth buying right now, whether you’ve got the latest Pro Max or an older model that still does the job.
 How We Selected
 When researching picks, we made sure each one delivers fast charging suited to the range of what current iPhones can take, from the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max at 60 watts, to the iPhone 17 at 40 watts, down to the iPhone 15 and 16 at around 20 to 27 watts. Each recommendation supports the right standard for the job, USB-C Power Delivery for wired charging and Qi2 or Qi2.2 for wireless. We stuck with brands we’ve used before and that back their products with warranties. Everything here is widely available across major retailers, including Amazon.

 Apple’s dynamic adapter is a USB-C brick that runs around 40 watts most of the time and ramps up to 60 when a device needs it, using Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) to match power demand. It’s small for what it delivers, about 3.2 ounces, with a matte white shell and prongs that fold flat so it slips into a bag or pocket. Smart thermal management holds its output steady through a long charge rather than throttling back as it heats up. There’s only one port, so it charges a single device at a time, but it’s the most dependable way to get full wired speed from Apple’s newest iPhone.

 At roughly the size of an ice cube, the Anker Nano Charger delivers up to 30 watts using gallium nitride (GaN) internals, enough to fast-charge any recent iPhone and even provide power to an iPad Air or MacBook Air in a pinch. It weighs under two ounces, the prongs fold flat, and ActiveShield thermal monitoring keeps it cool. It supports Programmable Power Supply (PPS), so it plays nicely with phone from other brands, too, and it comes in five colors. Like most chargers here, the USB-C cable is sold separately. It won’t hit the iPhone 18 Pro’s absolute peak speed, but for around $15, it’s great to have on hand.

 Why add a display to your charger? Well, it can show real-time charging status. The charger recognizes your iPhone model automatically and tunes its output to match, with a Care Mode that runs the battery cooler for overnight charging. The prongs also fold two ways and rotate a full 180 degrees, so you can plug it into an awkward or sideways outlet and still angle the screen to face you.
 A single USB-C port delivers up to 45 watts, and the whole thing is about 47 percent smaller than a standard 30-watt charger. With a top output of 45 watts, it falls short of the 60 the iPhone 18 Pro wants, so it charges fast but not at the phone’s absolute peak. Anker also has an updated version available for preorder that adds AVS adaptive charging and built-in iPhone 18 recognition through an app update.

 This is the charger to get for a desk where a laptop, phone, and tablet all want power at the same time. It has three ports—two USB-C and one USB-A—set on the side rather than the bottom, which keeps the weight of your cables from tugging it out of the outlet. A laptop plugged into one of the USB-C ports can pull the full 100 watts on its own, enough to fast-charge a MacBook Air or most 14-inch laptops , and the charger reallocates power as you add or unplug devices. Small icons next to the ports show which one delivers the highest output, so you know where to plug the laptop.
 Like the Nano Charger above, Anker’s 100W USB-C Charger has a screen, and you can rotate the readout to face you whichever way the charger sits on the outlet. Once more than one device is connected, the 100 watts gets split automatically, so a glance tells you when your laptop has dropped in charging speeds because a tablet is sharing the load, or confirms your phone is fast-charging rather than trickling from a bad cable. Thankfully, Anker includes a USB-C cable in the box.

 This is the one to leave on a nightstand, since it powers your iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods from a single base, and it comes with a wall adapter in the box. The magnetic pad delivers the full 25 watts of Qi2.2 to an iPhone 16 or later, while an iPhone 15 tops out at 15 watts. What separates it from most 3-in-1 stands is a fast-charging Apple Watch puck instead of a slow generic coil, so a Series 10 or later reaches 80 percent in about 45 minutes.
 The phone pad tilts for the iPhone’s StandBy mode, so it doubles as a bedside clock, and the pad has a built-in fan that helps with heat dissipation. It also features a relatively compact design. A lot of 3-in-1 stands sprawl sideways and take up a lot of space, but this places the Apple Watch puck in the back, along with a third charging pad for AirPods in the base.

 At barely half an inch thick, this magnetic bank snaps onto the back of an iPhone. It charges wirelessly at the full 25 watts of Qi2.2 with an iPhone 16 or later, while older models top out at 15 watts, and its 10,000mAh capacity holds close to two full iPhone charges. A short USB-C cord clips on as a wrist lanyard and pulls off when you want faster wired charging, up to 45 watts, enough to take an iPhone 17 Pro from empty to around 50 percent in about 25 minutes. A tiny digital display shows how much charge is left, and it supports pass-through, so you can refill the charger and your phone at the same time.

 Instead of tossing a separate cord in your bag, Anker’s Nano Power Bank has a built-in retractable USB-C cable, so you don’t have to worry about carrying a cable with you. It puts out up to 45 watts, enough to fast-charge an iPhone, and a small display shows live wattage, how much charge is left, and the battery’s long-term health.
 A second USB-C port and a USB-A sit alongside the built-in cable, so you can charge a few devices at once. It also supports pass-through charging, allowing you to charge the battery and your phone at the same time. The compact design makes it easy to throw in a bag, and it’s flight-approved, so you can have it ready in your carry-on.
 What to Consider
 The charging speed your iPhone can achieve depends on the model you own. Apple rates each recent iPhone by how quickly it refills with a large enough adapter. An iPhone 15 or 16 reaches about 50 percent in 30 minutes from a 20-watt adapter or higher, the iPhone 17 does it in roughly 20 minutes with about a 40-watt adapter, and the iPhone 18 Pro reaches 50 percent in about 15 minutes, but only with a 60-watt-capable adapter that supports PD 3.1 with AVS.
 For nearly everyone a 30-watt charger is enough, and it can also charge an iPad or a small laptop. Whatever you buy, check whether a cable is included and that it’s rated to support the speeds your phone needs. For instance, the iPhone 18 Pro’s fastest speed requires a 60-watt-capable USB-C cable. An older cable can reduce charging speed even on a good charger, so you may want to consider a new one to use with your setup.
 A single-port adapter is all most people need, but a multi-port charger is useful if your setup includes a laptop, tablet, and a phone. Note that a multi-port charger divides its total wattage among the ports, so a 100-watt three-port charger will not deliver the full 100 watts to a laptop once other devices are attached. Chargers built with GaN run cooler and fit more power into a smaller body than older silicon models, so a 100-watt charger can now be small enough to carry every day, and a foldable plug helps if you travel or work remotely.
 On the wireless side, MagSafe and Qi2 are the most convenient way to charge and a good choice for a nightstand or a desk. They reach 25 watts on an iPhone 16 or later (with a 30-watt adapter or higher) and 15 watts on the iPhone 15. If you’re after convenience, wireless is a good option, especially overnight when you don’t need the phone charged as fast as possible.
 While fast charging is convenient for a quick top up, the higher heat can shorten a battery’s lifespan over time, so for a phone left charging overnight, a slower or actively cooled charger reduces long-term wear. Look for basic protections such as over-temperature and over-current cutoffs, and for wireless chargers, choose Qi2 or MagSafe-certified models from established brands.

results.title: iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15: Should you upgrade?
results.snippet: The iPhone 17 is a substantial upgrade over the iPhone 15, though the older model remains capable. Both launched at $799, but the iPhone 17 includes 256GB of storage versus 128GB on the iPhone 15. Its 6.3-inch OLED display adds an adaptive 120Hz refresh rate, making scrolling and gaming noticeably smoother, while brightness is only modestly higher in testing. The A19 chip significantly outperforms the iPhone 15’s A16 Bionic in benchmarks, although everyday performance gains are less dramatic.  For most of us, the days of upgrading to a new phone every year are long gone. And that makes comparisons like an iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 face-off especially valuable. Stacking up the two phones side by side can help you see if the new model offers enough improvements to justify an upgrade or whether you're better off sticking with your current phone.
 Certainly, the iPhone 15 has a lot of life left in it, even if it's now more than two years old. The A16 Bionic powering the phone remains a top performer, and the cameras on the iPhone 15 still produce excellent images. With the iOS 26 update installed, the iPhone 15 figures to be a very capable phone for at least another year or two.
 But this fall's iPhone 17 release shows just how much can change in two years. Not only is the display bigger than the one on the iPhone 15, you also get a faster refresh rate for the first time on Apple's entry-level flagship. Throw in the usual chipset and camera updates, plus the continued ability to run Apple Intelligence features, and the iPhone 17 feels like a big leap forward from the iPhone of two years ago.

 Apple used to keep older flagships around at reduced prices for up to two years after their release, but that's not the case with the iPhone 15. With the iPhone 16e now occupying that $599 slot in Apple's lineup, the iPhone 15 disappeared with the release of the iPhone 17 in September.

 Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.
 iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 design 
 (Image credit: Future) In general, the look of the iPhone hasn't changed that much from the iPhone 15 to the iPhone 17, with the same slab design and rounded corners. Flip the phone over and you'll notice that the camera layout has changed — instead of the diagonally aligned main and ultrawide lenses of the iPhone 15, the iPhone 17 stacks its cameras on top of one another. That change, introduced with last year's iPhone 16 , allows you to capture spatial photos and videos with the newer phone.
 The iPhone 16 introduced two other design changes that continue with the iPhone 17 — a Camera Control button on the right side of the phone and an Action button on the left replacing the Mute switch. The Camera Control button serves as a shortcut for launching the iPhone's camera, and it can also access the Visual Intelligence feature that turns your camera into a search tool. I think so little of the button, I've disabled Camera Control , so I don't think iPhone 15 owners are missing out here.
 iPhone 17 (Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco) The Action button is a different story. You can press it to silence your phone, or you can set the button to trigger a specific shortcut, from turning on the flashlight to launching the iPhone's Focus mode feature to minimize distractions. It's a nice addition for personalizing your iPhone for the tasks you turn to the most.

 Apple has also made its iPhone more durable over time, with the iPhone 17 using Ceramic Shield 2 to protect the device's display. The new version is 3x more scratch resistant than the original Ceramic Shield found on the iPhone 15.
 The iPhone 17 has a larger screen, making the new model fractionally taller than the iPhone 15, though other dimensions are essentially the same. The 6.24-ounce iPhone 17 does outweigh its two-year-old predecessor by 0.22 ounces.
 iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 display 
 (Image credit: Future) About that larger screen: the iPhone 17 features a 6.3-inch display compared to 6.1 inches on the iPhone 15. It's not a huge difference, though when I watched the "Wicked: For Good" trailer on both phones, the iPhone 17's wider viewing area certainly feels more expansive.
 The bigger change is that Apple now turns to a Super Retina XDR panel for the iPhone 17, which means the screen's refresh rate can adapt based on what's happening on your phone. As a result, text scrolls more smoothly and game graphics feels more immersive than it does on the iPhone 15 and its 60Hz panel. In my opinion, the 120Hz refresh rate on the iPhone 17 practically justifies an upgrade all on its own.

 The iPhone 17 promises a brighter display, with a listed peak brightness of 3,000 nits to the iPhone 15's 2,000-nit max. In reality, the numbers are a lot closer, with the iPhone 17 outshining the iPhone 15 by 1,505 nits to 1,401 nits in our testing. Color reproduction numbers are virtually indistinguishable between the two displays.
 iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 cameras 
 (Image credit: Future) Apple has been tinkering with its camera setup since the iPhone 15 came out, and the end result should be better photos in more scenarios if you use the iPhone 17. While both phones still offer a 48MP main lens, the iPhone 17 replaces the 12MP ultrawide camera on the iPhone 15 with a second 48MP sensor. That should mean more detailed ultrawide shots, as well as better macro close-ups with the iPhone 17.
 Up front, the 12MP TrueDepth camera on the iPhone 15 makes way for an 18MP Center Stage lens. Besides the higher megapixel rating, the Center Stage camera on the iPhone 17 has a square sensor to adjust the orientation of the shot without requiring you to reposition the phone.
 To gauge how the iPhone's cameras have progressed since 2023, I took a handful of shots with an iPhone 17 and iPhone 15, starting with this photo of my apple tree. Colors look vibrant in both shots, with a good blend of light and shadow. I do think the iPhone 17 does a better job highlighting the water droplet on one of the apples, which I'd chalk up to improvements the Fusion Main camera used on the newer model.
 The ultrawide shots of this old fighter jet look pretty similar, which surprised me given the jump in megapixels for the iPhone 17's camera. Both phones proved equally adept at calling out the blue patches in the cloudy sky, and there's a similar level of detail on the surface of the plane itself.
 That said, to my eye, the edges of the wing in the iPhone 17 shot look a little sharper, particularly on the far side. I wouldn't be dismissive of the iPhone 15's effort, though.
 My daughter took a pair of portrait shots to see what improvements Apple's made to that model over the years. And setting aside the slightly different shooting angles, I think the iPhone 17 has the better shot. My skin tone is warmer, while still realistic, and the background colors look a little more vibrant.
 A night shot of some stuffed animals is essentially a wash between the iPhone 17 and iPhone 15. The pink critter in the back is more evenly colored in the iPhone 17 photo if you want to nitpick, but both cameras excel in low light.
 Overall, I think the iPhone 17 takes better photos than the iPhone 15, though they're not significantly better. You'll have more tools at your disposal should you upgrade to the iPhone 17, but if you stick with your current phone, you're still going get some very well-composed shots.
 iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 performance and software 
 iPhone 17 (Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco) You'd expect the iPhone 17 to outmuscle the iPhone 15 simply because Apple's newer phone uses a chip that's several generations ahead of the silicon powering the older model. Indeed, the A19 system-on-chip inside the iPhone 17 doesn't disappoint, beating the iPhone 15's A16 Bionic chipset handily in both CPU and GPU benchmarks.
