 On Geekbench, the A19 beats the A16 Bionic's single core and multicore scores by 47% and 53%, respectively. The iPhone 17 can also churn out nearly 3x the frames per second as the iPhone 15 in 3DMark's Solar Bay Unlimited graphics test.
 That said, in terms of real-world results, the iPhone 17 only beat the iPhone 15 by 2 seconds in a video transcoding test. Clearly, the iPhone 17 offers a faster chip, but you could argue that the real-world performance gains won't be all that noticeable on many tasks. For a lot of people, the iPhone 15's performance remains good enough.
 There is one big difference between the two phones, though, even if both can run the latest version of iOS 26. The iPhone 17 supports Apple Intelligence, while the iPhone 15 does not, so the only way that iPhone 15 owners can experience Apple's AI tools is by upgrading to a newer phone.
 I argued at the time of the iPhone 16's release that the current crop of Apple Intelligence tools aren't impressive or vital enough to justify an upgrade all on their own. It's possible that changes in 2026 when Apple hopes to release a more intelligent version of its Siri assistant . But at that point, iPhone 15 owners might prefer to wait for the iPhone 18 release in the fall to reap the benefit of even more upgrades.
 iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 battery life and charging 
 iPhone 17 (Image credit: Tom's Guide / John Velasco) The entry-level iPhone has always struggled to match the battery life of Apple's larger phones, which have more internal space for a bigger battery. That's the case with the iPhone 17, which turns in a time of 12 hours and 47 minutes on our battery test. That's certainly respectable, but a far cry from the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max , which both landed spots on our best phone battery life list.
 Still, iPhone 15 users who upgrade to the iPhone 17 will be jumping to a phone that lasts longer on a charge. When we tested the iPhone 15, it held out for just 11 hours and 5 minutes on our test, a little better than the average smartphone these days.
 Even better, Apple has boosted the charging speeds on the iPhone 17. You can now enjoy wired charging speeds of 35W and 25W Qi 2.2 wireless charging. That compares to 20W and 15W, respectively, for the iPhone 15.
 iPhone 17 vs. iPhone 15 verdict 
 The iPhone 17 offers notable improvements to anyone upgrading from an iPhone 15, with a larger, faster refreshing display leading the changes. But you'll also get a better performing phone that lasts longer on a charger while also taking better photos on average. Though the ability to use Apple Intelligence features wouldn't push me to upgrade, it is a nice bonus that guarantees future enhancements to your phone courtesy of software updates.
 I think people who want to squeeze as much use out of their phone as possible before upgrading won't feel cheated should they stick with the older model. But the advantages offered by the iPhone 17 are pretty stark when you take a closer look at the two phones.

 More Pro than ever 
 Apple is blurring the lines between base and Pro models with the iPhone 17, and it's more capable than ever. You get new cameras, 120Hz and AOD support, and a new A19 processor. Plus, there's Ceramic Shield 2 cover glass with an anti-reflective coating.

 The Samsung Galaxy S25 can do it all despite its smaller form factor. It has a best-in-class Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite for Galaxy chipset, excellent software and AI features, and a telephoto camera. However, the design and camera hardware overall is a few years old. 
 Pros

 Apple has a new crop of smartphones, and the iPhone 17 feels like the first base model in years to be truly competitive with the best Android phones. In the past, it was easy to criticize Apple for seemingly holding back basic features, like always-on displays and high refresh rates, from the cheapest new iPhone. The iPhone 17 flips the script, adding both of those long-awaited features and a whole lot more to make the base model eye-catching.
 For those looking for a small and cheap flagship, the Samsung Galaxy S25 has looked great on paper for the past few years. It's the most compact out of the top options from Apple, Samsung, and Google, and it added a third rear camera before it was cool. Now, it's time to see whether the iPhone 17 can beat the Galaxy S25 at its own game in base-model value.
 iPhone 17 vs. Samsung Galaxy S25: Design and display
 (Image credit: Apple) The iPhone 17 and the Galaxy S25 are both small flagships, but Apple's smartphone is heavier and less compact than Samsung's. It comes down to the displays — Samsung is still using a 6.2-inch AMOLED panel on the Galaxy S25, whereas Apple moved to a larger 6.3-inch screen. Both are now capable of hitting 120Hz refresh rates, and have AOD options.
 Latest Videos From Android Central 
 Watch full video here: 
 Apple is using Ceramic Shield 2 glass on the iPhone 17, and Samsung opted for Gorilla Glass Victus 2 on the Galaxy S25. Both are made by Corning, but the key difference is that the iPhone 17's cover glass is optimized for scratch protection and has anti-reflective properties. To get an anti-reflective screen on a Samsung Galaxy phone, you have to go with the expensive Galaxy S25 Ultra model.
 (Image credit: Brady Snyder / Android Central) It's hard to understate the difference in size between the iPhone 17 and Galaxy S25. By just comparing the screen sizes, the gap looks minuscule, but there's more to the story. The iPhone measures 149.6 x 71.5 x 8mm and weighs 177 grams, which is larger by every measure compared to the Galaxy S25's dimensions of 146.9 x 70.5 x 7.2 mm. The Samsung base model's weight is particularly impressive at just 162 grams — even lighter than the iPhone Air .

 Apple iPhone Duo vs. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8: It comes down to just one thing 
 Surprisingly, the Galaxy S25 packs flagship specs and a larger battery capacity than the iPhone 17 in that small form factor. The only key compromise here is the display, which is smaller by one tenth of an inch. Only you can decide whether the bigger, thicker, and heavier design of the iPhone 17 is a dealbreaker, but I prefer the compact and lightweight build of the Galaxy S25.
 (Image credit: Apple) As for durability, both phones sport an IP68 certification against dust and water ingress. They're also made out of aluminum and have frosted glass backs.

 iPhone 17 vs. Samsung Galaxy S25: Hardware and specs
 (Image credit: Brady Snyder / Android Central) Apple and Samsung both equipped their cheapest flagship phones with current-generation processors, but the Galaxy S25 goes a step further. It's powered by the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite for Galaxy mobile platform, the same one that powers Samsung's most expensive handsets. Meanwhile, the iPhone 17 runs on an Apple A19 chip that's a lower-tier offering compared to the A19 Pro in the Air and Pro models. This could help the Galaxy S25 excel in AI tasks and gaming, but that remains to be seen.
 Samsung has the advantage in on-device memory, with 12GB of RAM on the Galaxy S25 compared to the iPhone 17's 8GB. However, the iPhone 17 crucially starts with 256GB of base storage at the same price as the 128GB Galaxy S25. There's more storage available on the higher-end configurations, too. You can buy an iPhone 17 with up to 512GB of storage, while the Galaxy S25 tops out at 256GB.

The iPhone 17 does support Bluetooth 6 compared to Bluetooth 5.4 on the Galaxy S25 . On the flip side, the Galaxy S25 has a physical SIM tray, and all iPhones are eSIM-only in the U.S.

 Samsung gave the Galaxy S25 slightly more battery life, but it charges more slowly and doesn't have internal magnets for Qi2 or MagSafe. The iPhone 17 can now do 40-60W fast wired charging and take advantage of Qi2.2 25W wireless charging, which is great to see.
 (Image credit: Apple) While the A19 chip is a capable performer, Samsung likely does more with its on-device Galaxy AI processing than Apple does with Apple Intelligence at the moment. Between Galaxy AI and Gemini , the Galaxy S25 has the more robust AI suite.
 iPhone 17 vs. Samsung Galaxy S25: Cameras
 (Image credit: Apple) The iPhone 17 received a few major camera upgrades this year, headlined by the 18MP selfie camera. This new camera lens now uses a square sensor, a shift from typical 4:3 sensor. The practical benefit of this change is being able to take selfies in either orientation, portrait or landscape, without having to physically rotate your phone. And when there's a big group shot, Center Stage uses AI to automatically expand the view to fit everyone in.
 The rear cameras are a bit less exciting — they're 48MP sensors, a main and an ultrawide. Still, they look to perform great and provide the stabilization and video recording Apple is known for.
 (Image credit: Brady Snyder / Android Central) Samsung has an extra rear telephoto lens, which adds a 3x optical zoom length into the mix. It's the handy tool in a triple-camera system that also consists of a 50MP, f/1.8 main sensor and a 12MP, f/2.2 ultrawide with a 120-degree field of view. Google followed suit this year, adding a telephoto camera to its base-model Pixel 10, but Samsung pioneered this offering on cheaper flagships.
 Compared to the 2x optical-quality zoom the iPhone 17 achieves using sensor crop, the Galaxy S25's true 3x optical zoom will undoubtedly produce better results.
 iPhone 17 vs. Samsung Galaxy S25: Which should you buy
 (Image credit: Apple) The iPhone 17 and Samsung Galaxy S25 are more similar than you may think — both feature the same chassis design as older models and come with key limitations compared to their higher-end counterparts. However, both also stand out in their own way. Aside from the obvious iOS 26 vs. One UI 7 debate, these phones focus on completely different things.
 The iPhone 17 clearly puts an emphasis on the cameras, making it a great option for creators or anyone who loves to take photos or videos. Yes, it has one fewer rear camera than the Galaxy S25, but its 48MP main and ultrawide cameras are top-notch. Plus, the square front-facing camera that makes it possible to capture vertical or horizontal selfies without rotating your device is a standout feature.
 Meanwhile, the Galaxy S25 has more raw power with the Snapdragon 8 Elite for Galaxy chipset, and it does more with it thanks to Galaxy AI and Gemini . It'll run circles around Apple Intelligence, and the smarts may even help the phone beat the iPhone 17 in gaming and intensive tasks.
 You can't go wrong with either one, but if you happen to care about camera or AI features, you may want to pick the iPhone 17 or Galaxy S25, respectively.

Qi2.2 25W Wireless Charging in 2026: A Compatibility and Buying Guide
SEPTEMBER 15, 2026
Share

Category: Desk Setup & Charging TechSeptember 15, 202612 min read

Quick answer: The best Qi2.2 charger for a 2026 flagship is not chosen by the wattage printed on the box alone. Check four things together: the phone's actual Qi2 profile, magnetic alignment, the charger's power input, and whether the stand can charge the rest of your device ecosystem. Qi2.2 25W is becoming a practical upgrade for compatible phones, but a certified 25W charger can still behave like a slower charger when the phone, case, adapter, or temperature does not support the same power path.

This guide turns the 2026 flagship launch cycle into a simple buying decision for iPhone 18, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8, Pixel 11, and other Qi2-compatible phones.

A 25W Qi2.2 charging station is most useful when it combines stable magnetic alignment with a clear place for every device.

Chapter 1: What the 2026 Qi2.2 News Means for Buyers

Wireless charging has moved from a phone accessory feature to an ecosystem decision. The 2026 phone cycle is making that shift more visible: new flagship devices, foldables, watches, earbuds, magnetic cases, and multi-device stands all compete for the same space on a desk or nightstand.

The important industry story is not simply that a new charger can advertise 25W. The useful change is that higher-power magnetic charging is becoming easier to evaluate. Buyers can now ask whether a product is certified, whether the phone supports the relevant profile, and whether the complete charging chain has enough input power and thermal headroom.

That distinction matters because a charger can be technically capable while the real-world setup is not. A thick case can weaken alignment. A low-power USB-C adapter can cap output. A folded phone may place its coil away from the charging area. A hot desk or direct sunlight can trigger thermal control. The best buying guide therefore starts with the whole use case, not a single specification.

Chapter 2: Qi2.2 25W Specifications That Actually Matter

Use this table before comparing brands. It separates the words used in product listings from the checks that affect the experience you will get at home or at work.

Buying factor	What to check	Why it matters
Qi2 certification	Look for a clear certification claim and model information. Treat “Qi2-style” or “magnetic wireless” as different claims.	Certification gives you a better starting point for interoperability and safety. It does not guarantee that every phone reaches 25W.
Phone support	Confirm the phone's official wireless charging profile and the supported power level.	The phone controls the negotiated charging rate. A 25W charger cannot force a non-25W phone to charge at 25W.
Magnetic alignment	Check whether the phone has built-in magnets or needs a compatible magnetic case or ring.	Stable alignment reduces disconnects and makes charging easier to use while reading, taking calls, or filming.
USB-C input	Match the recommended adapter wattage and protocol. For multi-device stands, calculate total output rather than phone output alone.	A phone plus watch plus earbuds can exceed the capacity of a small adapter.
Thermal design	Prefer a charger with a substantial contact surface, airflow around the phone, and sensible power management.	Heat is a normal reason for charging speed to change during a long session.
Stand geometry	Check viewing angle, hinge stability, landscape support, and whether a camera bump prevents a flat fit.	A charger is part of the desk workflow. It should hold the phone where you can use it.
Apple problem background: one charger for the iPhone 18 routine

For an iPhone user, the problem is usually not finding a magnetic pad. It is keeping the phone, Apple Watch, and earbuds charged without three separate cables taking over the desk or bedside table.

Recommended answer: Elecdov CE19A 3-in-1 Apple Charging Station. The product workbook classifies CE19A under Apple, and its 3-in-1 format matches the phone-plus-watch-plus-earbuds use case described in this guide.

Data and comparison: a single-device pad uses one charging position and solves the phone problem only. A 3-in-1 station consolidates three charging positions into one desk zone, so it is the better fit when all three devices are part of the user's daily carry. The product page should be used to confirm the current iPhone, Watch, case, and power-adapter compatibility before purchase.

Final answer: choose CE19A when the primary phone is an iPhone and the same location also needs Apple Watch and earbuds charging. Choose a single pad instead when the user only needs phone charging.

Summary: CE19A is recommended here because the product category matches Apple and the 3-in-1 structure directly addresses the multi-device problem. It is not being presented as a universal Samsung or Google recommendation.

Samsung problem background: stable charging for Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8

Foldable Galaxy phones add a physical constraint to wireless charging: the phone's weight, hinge, camera bump, case, and folded or unfolded position can change how securely it sits on a magnetic stand. The main problem is dependable alignment during calls, notifications, and desk use.

Recommended answer: Elecdov W103S Samsung Magnetic Qi2 Charger. The product workbook places W103S in the Samsung category, making it the relevant brand-matched recommendation for this section.

Data and comparison: compare a phone-only magnetic charger with a 3-in-1 station by checking the actual phone position, case thickness, and the number of devices charged at the same time. W103S is the correct starting point for a Samsung-focused setup, but the Galaxy model, regional variant, case, and supported charging profile still determine the real result. A product category is not a substitute for an exact model fit test.

Final answer: choose W103S when Samsung compatibility and a multi-device station are the priority. Before scaling the setup, test the exact Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Z Flip 8 case in both the charging orientation and the viewing orientation used most often.

Summary: W103S is recommended because it is listed as a Samsung product and directly addresses the article's Samsung alignment problem. The recommendation does not claim that every foldable reaches the same wattage or holds in every case.

Google problem background: a Pixel charging hub that reduces cable swapping

Pixel users often need a charging dock that keeps the phone visible for checking notifications while simultaneously charging the watch and storing small household items. The key decision lies in whether to use a compatible magnetic case for the phone or opt for a different Qi charging solution.

Recommended answer: Elecdov WC01G Google 2-in-1 Magnetic Charging Station. The product workbook classifies WC01G under Google, so it is the correct Google-family recommendation for the Pixel section.

Data and comparison: For users who need to charge their watches and store various accessories, a 2-in-1 charging station is more efficient than a standalone charging pad, as it utilizes a designated charging area and a single power adapter connection. If your Pixel model or case does not support magnetic alignment, please check for compatible cases or use the product's non-magnetic charging position where applicable. Do not assume that standard Qi charging implies support for Qi2 magnetic functionality.

Final answer: If your primary phone is a Google Pixel and your daily routine involves charging the watch and organizing your devices, please choose the WC01G. Before checking out, be sure to verify the specific Pixel model, phone case, and charger input requirements on the product page.

Summary: The WC01G is recommended because the product list identifies it as a Google product, and its 2-in-1 design solves the Pixel charging and storage issues described here.

Elecdov selection rule

Choose the highest output that your phone and adapter can use consistently, then prioritize alignment and daily access. A stable 15W or 20W setup is often more useful than a 25W charger that disconnects because the case or stand geometry is wrong.

Magnetic alignment is the practical part of Qi2: it helps the phone stay centered while the user keeps the screen visible.

Chapter 3: Compatibility Guide for iPhone 18, Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Flip 8, and Pixel 11

Phone launches create search spikes, but product names are not enough to select a charger. Use the device's official technical page as the final authority, especially when a model has regional variants or a new foldable form factor. The right question is not “Does this phone support wireless charging?” It is “Does my phone, case, stand, and adapter work together in the position I use?”

Chapter 4: How to Choose the Charger and Power Adapter

Step 1: Define the number of devices

For phone-only charging, a compact magnetic pad or folding stand is enough. For a phone, watch, and earbuds, a 3-in-1 station reduces cable swaps and keeps the desk readable. For a phone plus a tablet or laptop, use a separate USB-C power path and do not treat a small wireless stand as the main power supply.

Read the charger's input recommendation and add the expected load of every active pad or USB port. Leave headroom for efficiency losses. If a charger is advertised as 25W for the phone but also charges two other devices, ask how output is distributed when all positions are occupied.

Chapter 5: Best Qi2.2 Setup by Daily Scenario
For a professional desk

Use a raised stand with a clear viewing angle. Keep the charging area beside, rather than underneath, the keyboard and mouse. The phone should be reachable for a call without forcing you to unplug it. Add a 3-in-1 base when the watch and earbuds would otherwise create two more cables.

For a calm bedside

Prioritize stable low-glare design, a clear clock or indicator policy, and easy one-handed placement. Do not place a bright charging display directly in your line of sight. Cable routing matters as much as charging speed because the bedside is where loose wires become visual noise.

For business travel

Choose a folding stand that can fit beside a hotel lamp or on a narrow café table. Pack one compatible USB-C adapter and one short cable. Confirm the charger's voltage input and carry-on requirements for any battery-powered companion product separately; a wireless charger is not automatically a power bank.

For mobile creators

Magnetic alignment is valuable when the phone is used as a monitor, teleprompter, navigation screen, or camera control. Look for a hinge that stays fixed during touch input and enough ventilation around the phone. For longer recording sessions, expect the phone to reduce charging speed if heat builds up.

Chapter 7: FAQ and Final Buying Checklist

Q: Does a 25W Qi2.2 charger make every phone charge at 25W?

No. The phone, charger, adapter, case, and thermal conditions all affect the negotiated rate. Treat 25W as the charger's output class, then verify the phone's official support.

Q: Is Qi2 the same as MagSafe?

They are related magnetic charging ecosystems, but they are not interchangeable marketing terms. Check the phone and accessory maker's compatibility statement, especially for maximum power and magnetic attachment.

Q: Can I use a Qi2.2 charger with a Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Z Flip 8?

Check the exact model, case, coil position, and magnetic support. A foldable may charge wirelessly while still needing a compatible magnetic case or a stand with better physical support.

Q: What adapter should I use?

Use the USB-C adapter recommended for the charger and size it for the total number of active outputs. A multi-device station needs more headroom than a phone-only pad.
